cloud.title: Cloud Fundamental
cloud.deck: Platform names change. The parts do not: a place to run, a place to store, a network, an identity, and a bill. These notes stay on that shared model.

sections.label: The cloud model
sections.html:
The cloud model

A cloud provider runs large pools of machines, disks, and networks, and rents slices of them through an API. You stop ordering hardware for each new service. You start describing what you want, and you pay for what stays switched on.

Elasticity is the ability to add or remove capacity. Scalability is the ability of the design to handle growth at all. A single large virtual machine can be scaled up until it cannot. An elastic design adds copies and later removes them.

How much of the stack you still operate.
ModelYou manageProvider manages
Infrastructure as a serviceOperating system, runtime, application, dataHardware, hypervisor, the physical network
Platform as a serviceApplication and dataRuntime patching, the machines underneath
Software as a serviceConfiguration, users, and the data you uploadThe application itself

Places

A region is a group of data centers in a geography. An availability zone is an isolated group inside that region, with separate power and network. Putting two copies in one zone protects you from a bad deploy. Putting them in two zones protects you from a building. Putting them in two regions protects you from a region, and it costs more in latency, data transfer, and operational work.

The account, subscription, or project is the blast-radius boundary. Production and experiments should not share one. Bills, permissions, and quotas attach to that boundary.

sections.label: Compute
sections.html:
Compute

Compute is anything that runs your code. The useful split is how long it lives and what you must patch.

  • Virtual machines look like servers. You choose the size, the image, and usually the operating system patches. They fit long-running processes, licensed software, and lift-and-shift.
  • Containers package a process and its dependencies. You still need something to run the containers: a service, or a cluster you operate. They fit when many services should share the same deployment shape.
  • Functions run for one event or request, then disappear. The provider patches the runtime. They fit irregular traffic and glue between services. They fit poorly when you need a long-held connection, local disk, or a cold start that breaks the latency budget.

Stateless compute is easier to scale. Put durable data in a store, not on the instance disk. An instance can disappear in a replacement, a scale-in, or a zone failure. If the only copy of a file lived there, it is gone.

Scale out by adding copies when the work can be split. Scale up by buying a bigger machine when the work cannot. Most "just make it bigger" stories end when the biggest size is still not enough.

sections.label: Storage
sections.html:
Storage

Pick storage from the access pattern, not from the product name.

Three shapes, three jobs.
ShapeLooks likeGood for
BlockA disk attached to a machineDatabases and anything that expects a filesystem on one host
FileA shared filesystemSeveral machines reading the same tree
ObjectA key and a blob, reached over HTTPUploads, backups, images, data files, static sites

Object storage is durable because the provider keeps copies. It is not a POSIX disk, and it is not a database. You do not edit a byte in the middle. You write a new object.

A managed database is someone else's operational work: patching, backups, and often failover. You still own schema, indexes, query shape, and the decision about what the data means. Running the database yourself is reasonable when you need a specific version, extension, or placement. It is an ongoing job, not a checkbox.

Copies

Durability is "the provider did not lose the bits." Availability is "you can read them now." A backup is a separate copy you can restore, preferably in another region, with a tested restore. A replica that accepts the same bad write as the primary is not a backup.

sections.label: Networking
sections.html:
Networking

A virtual network is your address space inside the provider. Subnets divide it. Routes and security rules decide what may talk. Private subnets have no direct route from the internet. Public ones do, and that should be a small set: load balancers and bastions, not every application server.

  • Load balancer. Spreads traffic across healthy copies and gives callers one address. Health checks must match real readiness, or the balancer will send users to a process that is up and useless.
  • DNS. Turns names into addresses. Use it for failover only when you have measured how long caches keep the old answer.
  • TLS. Protects the hop you terminate. Termination at the load balancer is common. Traffic behind it should still be restricted, and sometimes encrypted again, depending on who else shares the network.

Egress is easy to forget in the design and obvious on the bill. Data leaving a region, or leaving the provider toward the internet, is often priced differently from data staying inside. A chatty service that pulls from another region on every request will show up as cost before it shows up as latency you noticed.

Draw trust boundaries first: internet, your network, the data store, the management plane. Then place controls on the lines you actually cross.

sections.label: Identity and access
sections.html:
Identity and access

Every call is made by someone or something. Users are people. Workloads are the programs: a virtual machine, a function, a pipeline. They should not share an account. A person leaving the team is not the same event as rotating what a service uses.

  • Grant the smallest permission that lets the job finish. Wide roles feel faster until a leaked key can do everything the admin can do.
  • Prefer short-lived credentials issued to the workload. Long-lived keys in a repository or a laptop are a common breach path.
  • Federate human login to one identity provider so joiners and leavers are handled in one place.
  • Separate the permission to change infrastructure from the permission to read production data.

Audit logs answer "who did what." Turn them on before you need them, and send them somewhere the same account cannot quietly delete. A trail that the attacker can erase is a diary, not evidence.

Identity is the real perimeter. Network rules still matter, but a valid key from anywhere will walk past a diagram that only shows firewalls.

sections.label: Cost and responsibility
sections.html:
Cost and responsibility

The shared responsibility model is the contract under the marketing. The provider secures the cloud: buildings, hardware, the hypervisor. You secure what you put in it: accounts, data, network exposure, and most configuration. On infrastructure as a service you patch the guest operating system. On functions the provider patches the platform, and you still own the code and the permissions it runs with.

Where money goes

  • Compute that is on while idle. Stop it, or size it to the real load.
  • Storage you forgot: old snapshots, unused disks, logs with no expiry.
  • Data transfer across regions and out to the internet.
  • Over-provisioned managed services left at their default size.

Tag resources with the system and the environment so a bill can be read. Set a budget alert before the month closes. A quota protects the account from a runaway loop. A budget alert tells a person.

Deleting an experiment is part of the design. If you cannot say who owns a resource, you cannot say whether it should still be running.

kubernetes.title: Kubernetes
kubernetes.deck: Kubernetes keeps a cluster moving toward the state you declared. These notes cover the objects you actually write, and the habits that make a cluster operable.

sections.label: The cluster picture
sections.html:
The cluster picture

A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane and a set of worker nodes. You submit a desired state, usually as YAML: "three copies of this container, reachable under this name." Controllers watch the current state and try to close the gap. That loop is the product. SSH into a node is a debugging tool, not the way you make a change stick.

The API server is the front door. etcd stores the cluster data. Schedulers place pods onto nodes that have room. Kubelets on each node start the containers the scheduler assigned. You can run this yourself, or you can use a managed control plane and still own the workloads, the identity, and the network policy.

If a change is not in the manifest that Git holds, the next reconcile can erase it. The cluster is a mirror. The repository is the source.

Labels are the join key

Kubernetes does not wire objects by memory address. A Service selects pods by labels. A network rule selects pods by labels. Spend the time to make labels boring and consistent: application, component, environment. A typo in a selector looks like "the app is down" when the app is running and invisible.

sections.label: Pods
sections.html:
Pods

A pod is the smallest thing you deploy. It is one or more containers that share a network namespace, which means they share localhost, and they can share volumes. Containers in a pod are started, scheduled, and die together. Most pods hold one application container. A second container is justified when it must share the pod's files or network: a proxy sidecar, or a helper that refreshes a certificate into a shared volume.

Pods are ephemeral. The disk inside the container goes away with the pod unless you mounted a volume. The pod IP changes when the pod is replaced. Callers should use a Service name, not a pod IP they happened to see.

Probes

  • Startup tells the kubelet the process is still booting, so a slow start is not mistaken for a deadlock.
  • Readiness tells the Service whether this pod should receive traffic. Fail it when a dependency you need is down.
  • Liveness restarts the container. Use it for a stuck process. Do not use it for a downed database, or the cluster will restart healthy code in a loop.

Requests and limits

A CPU or memory request is what the scheduler reserves. A limit is what the container is allowed to use. Without requests, the scheduler can pack a node until everything is slow. A memory limit that is too low kills the process. Set requests from a measurement, not from a guess you copy between services.

sections.label: Workloads
sections.html:
Workloads

You rarely create pods by hand. A workload controller creates them and replaces them when they disappear.

Choose the controller from identity and lifetime, not from habit.
ControllerUse when
DeploymentYou want N interchangeable copies. A rolling update replaces them. This is the default for stateless HTTP services.
StatefulSetEach replica needs a stable name, ordered startup, or its own disk. Databases and queues often land here, and they still need care that a YAML file does not supply.
DaemonSetEvery node (or a selected set) should run one copy: log collectors, network agents.
JobThe work should run to completion, then stop.
CronJobThe work should run on a schedule. Make the task safe to run twice, because a retry will.

A Deployment owns a ReplicaSet, which owns the pods. Roll back the Deployment, not a single pod. Deleting a pod is a restart. It is not a rollback, and it is not a fix for a bad image.

Horizontal scaling adds pods. It only helps when one request does not need more resources than a single pod has, and when sessions are not trapped on one copy.

sections.label: Services and traffic
sections.html:
Services and traffic

Every pod can reach every other pod by IP, across nodes. That flat network is convenient and it is also a wide default. Treat it as a starting point, then restrict it when the cluster holds more than one trust level.

A Service gives a stable name to a changing set of pods.
TypeWho can use it
ClusterIPOther workloads inside the cluster. This is the normal choice.
NodePortA port on every node. Useful for demos and odd network setups, noisy as a public design.
LoadBalancerAn external load balancer from the platform, with its own address.

HTTP routing sits above Services. An Ingress, or a Gateway, maps host names and paths to Services and often terminates TLS. The controller behind that object is a separate install. The Ingress resource does nothing until a controller is watching it.

Cluster DNS resolves Service names. Prefer name.namespace.svc.cluster.local in documentation, and the short name name only from callers in the same namespace. Cross-namespace calls should be explicit so a rename is visible.

NetworkPolicy is a lock you add once you know the allowed paths. An empty policy that selects nothing protects nothing. A policy that selects pods and lists no ingress denies them.

sections.label: Configuration
sections.html:
Configuration

Keep configuration out of the image. The same image should run in a test namespace and in production, with different config. Bake the build identity into the image. Inject the environment at deploy time.

  • ConfigMap holds plain settings: feature flags, addresses, small files. It is not secret, and it is not a place for a large binary.
  • Secret holds credentials and keys. The value is base64-encoded in the API, which is encoding, not encryption. Encryption at rest is a cluster setting. Anyone who can read Secrets in the namespace can use them.
  • Environment variables are easy and frozen at process start. Mounted files can be updated without a restart if the application re-reads them. Pick the one the process actually supports.

Do not store live Secrets in a public Git repository. A common pattern is to commit encrypted or referenced secrets, and let a controller materialize the Kubernetes Secret in the cluster. The manifest you review should not contain the raw password.

A ConfigMap change does not restart pods by itself. If the process only reads the environment at startup, roll the workload or the new value will sit unused.

sections.label: Day-2 operations
sections.html:
Day-2 operations

The first deploy is the easy day. The cluster earns its cost on the days a node disappears, a rollout sticks, or a namespace runs out of memory.

Rollouts

A rolling update starts new pods before, or as, it stops old ones, depending on the surge and unavailable settings. Readiness must go green only when the new pod can serve. If readiness is always true, the rollout will happily replace a working version with a broken one. Keep the previous ReplicaSet so rollback is a declared change, not a scavenger hunt.

Namespaces and quotas

A namespace is a folder for names and a boundary for policy. It is not a strong security boundary by itself, but it is where you attach resource quotas, default limits, and who may deploy. Production and development on one cluster should at least be separate namespaces, with separate permissions. Many teams use separate clusters once the blast radius matters more than the extra cost.

What to look at

  • Events and pod status explain scheduling and crash loops.
  • Logs explain the process. Ship them off the node, because the node will be replaced.
  • Metrics explain saturation: CPU throttling, memory approaching the limit, restart counts.
  • A request id that crosses services explains a single failure better than a dashboard of averages.
kubectl is a window onto the API. Changes made only there will drift. Prefer a pull request that changes the manifest, then watch the controllers catch up.

ai-ml.title: AI / ML
ai-ml.deck: A model is one step in a pipeline. These notes follow the path from a decision you need, through data and evaluation, to a system that can be turned off safely.

sections.label: Map of the work
sections.html:
Map of the work

Machine learning builds a function from examples instead of writing every rule by hand. Artificial intelligence is the broader aim: systems that take on tasks we associate with judgment. Most useful systems are narrower than the aim. They classify, rank, forecast, or generate, inside a boundary someone chose.

A model is that function plus its parameters. It is the middle of a pipeline:

  1. Decide the action the system may take, and the cost of being wrong.
  2. Collect examples that match the moment of decision, not a convenient export.
  3. Train, then measure against a baseline a person could explain.
  4. Serve the model behind the same standards as any other dependency: latency, failure, and a way to roll back.
  5. Watch the inputs. A model does not announce that the world moved.
If a short rule or a query already makes the decision well, a model is extra machinery. Start there. Add learning when the rule table is what keeps breaking.

sections.label: Kinds of learning
sections.html:
Kinds of learning

The kind of learning follows from the feedback you have, not from whichever algorithm is popular this year.

Match the setup to the signal you can actually collect.
SetupThe signalTypical job
SupervisedEach example has a label or a target numberSpam or not, price, next value, "which class"
UnsupervisedNo labels, only the structure in the inputsGrouping, finding odd points, compressing
ReinforcementA reward after a sequence of actionsControl and game-like decisions, expensive to get right outside a simulator

A discriminative model scores or labels an input. A generative model draws new samples that resemble its training data. Generation is not understanding, and a fluent paragraph is not a checked fact. If the product needs a source of truth, put retrieval or a system of record next to the model and design for the case where they disagree.

Transfer learning starts from a model trained on a broad set and adapts it to a smaller one. It helps when your labeled set is thin and the broad model has seen similar inputs. It still needs an evaluation on your data. A leaderboard score is not that evaluation.

sections.label: Data and features
sections.html:
Data and features

Label quality beats model cleverness more often than notes like this admit. A clean definition of the label, written down, is part of the system. "Churn" that means three different things to three teams will train a model that is sure and useless.

Leakage

Leakage is when the training rows contain information that will not exist at decision time, or information that is the answer in disguise. A column copied from the outcome, a feature computed with the full future window, or a random split that puts the same user in both train and test: the offline score looks wonderful, and production looks ordinary.

Splits

  • Split by time when the world moves forward. Train on the past, test on a later period.
  • Split by entity when rows are repeated per user, device, or account, so the model cannot memorize an identity.
  • Random row splits are for independent rows. Most business tables are not independent rows.

A feature must be computable when you predict. If building it requires tomorrow's table, it is not a feature. It is a leak, or it is a batch job you have not scheduled. Document the freshness: how old the value may be, and what the model should do when it is missing.

Bias in the collection shows up as confidence later. Who is missing from the examples will be the group the metric does not describe.

sections.label: Training and evaluation
sections.html:
Training and evaluation

Training fits parameters to a training set. Evaluation asks whether the fit helps on data the fit did not see. Report the second number. Keep a baseline next to it: the majority class, the current rule, or a small linear model. A complex model that does not beat the baseline has not earned its operational cost.

Metrics follow the cost of errors

  • Accuracy hides failure when one class is rare. A model that always says "no fraud" can be 99% accurate and never catch a case.
  • Precision is the share of alarms that were right. Low precision trains people to ignore the system.
  • Recall is the share of real cases you caught. Low recall is silent miss.
  • Calibration asks whether a score of 0.8 is right about four times in five. Rankings can look fine while the probability is fiction. Do not show an uncalibrated score as a probability.

Slice the metric. An average can rise while a region, a language, or a customer tier gets worse. The slice you refuse to measure is the one that will page you.

Offline evaluation is a filter, not a launch. When the cost of a wrong action is high, shadow the model on live traffic, or send a small share of decisions, before it acts alone. Watch the decision, not only the loss curve.

sections.label: Serving
sections.html:
Serving

A trained file is not a service. Serving is an ordinary production problem with a versioned artifact in the middle.

  • Batch scores a table on a schedule. It fits when the decision can wait: nightly limits, morning lists.
  • Online scores one request inside a latency budget. It needs a feature lookup that is as fast as the model, and a timeout.
  • Fallback is the path when the model is slow, down, or unsure. A default rule, a previous score, or a human queue. Shipping without a fallback is shipping a hard dependency.

Version the model, the code that builds features, and the training data pointer together. A rollback that restores the model and leaves a new feature definition in place is not a rollback. Record the version on each prediction so a bad week can be traced.

After launch

Input drift means today's examples do not look like training. Prediction drift means the score distribution moved. Neither proves the decisions got worse, and a stable dashboard does not prove they stayed good. Keep a sample of outcomes, with a delay that matches how long the truth takes to arrive, and compare.

Cache a prediction only when the same inputs must yield the same action. Do not cache your way past a user who withdrew consent or a price that changed.

sections.label: Judgment and limits
sections.html:
Judgment and limits

A model repeats patterns in the data, including unfair ones and outdated ones. It does not know your policy. Policy has to be written beside it: who may be scored, what the score may change, and which decisions stay with a person.

  • State the intended use and the uses that are out of scope. A model fit for ranking search results is not a model fit for denying a service.
  • Treat training data as data you are accountable for. Private text, customer records, and scraped content do not become harmless because a training job consumed them.
  • Generated text can be confident and false. If you display it, give the reader a way to see the source, or do not present it as a record.
  • Keep a person responsible for the decision the system informs. "The model said so" is not an owner.
  • Plan to turn the model off. If the business cannot run the fallback for a day, you do not have a model in the loop. You have a single point of failure with a research name.
Measure harm on the groups affected, not only on the average user. A small overall error can still be a large error for the people with the least room to absorb it.

microservices.title: Microservices
microservices.deck: A microservice is a deployable boundary with its own data and its own reason to change. These notes stay on that boundary, not on a diagram full of boxes.

sections.label: The boundary
sections.html:
The boundary

Split a system where the business already splits. Orders, catalog, and billing change for different reasons and are often owned by different people. That is a candidate boundary. A function that is merely "small" is not.

Each service should be deployable without a lockstep release of the others. If every change still needs three teams to ship on the same day, the split is only a network hop.

Start with a modular codebase and a clear data owner. Extract a service when independent deploy is the pain you are relieving.

sections.label: Owned data
sections.html:
Owned data

A service owns the tables it writes. Other services ask it, or subscribe to what it publishes. They do not share its database. A shared database hides the coupling until a column rename takes the neighbors down.

  • One writer for each fact.
  • Copies elsewhere are caches or projections, with a known delay.
  • A transaction that must update two services is a design smell. Put the rule in one service, or accept a process that can be retried.

sections.label: Contracts
sections.html:
Contracts

The contract is the request, the response, and the errors a caller can handle. Write it down. A breaking change is a new version, or a field that callers can ignore until they are ready.

Do not leak your tables through the API. Return the words the caller needs. Internal names can change without a coordinated release.

sections.label: Calls between services
sections.html:
Calls between services

A synchronous call is simple and it couples availability. If the catalog is down, checkout waits. Use it when the caller cannot continue without the answer and the latency budget allows it.

An event is better when the receiver can act later. The publisher records that something happened. Consumers react, and they must tolerate duplicates and uncertain order. Name the event for the fact, not for the command you wish the other team would run.

sections.label: Failure
sections.html:
Failure

The network will drop calls, and a dependency will be slow. Time out. Limit how many calls you pile up. Decide the fallback: a cached answer, a smaller feature, or a clear error. Retry only when the operation is safe to run twice.

Give every request an id that crosses services. A dashboard of averages will not tell you which checkout failed.

devops.title: DevOps
devops.deck: DevOps is the habit of shipping a small change and knowing, quickly, whether it helped. These notes follow that loop from source to the running system.

sections.label: The loop
sections.html:
The loop

A change is not done when the code is merged. It is done when it is running, observed, and reversible. The same people who write the change should be able to see it fail and roll it back.

Small batches make that possible. A release that contains a month of work hides the cause. A release that contains one change tells you where to look.

sections.label: Build
sections.html:
Build

The build should be repeatable. Same source, same result. Pin the dependencies. Do not compile on a laptop and copy the artifact by hand.

  • One artifact, promoted through environments. Do not rebuild with different flags for production.
  • Tests that must pass before the artifact exists: unit checks, and a small set of contract checks.
  • A version you can point at: a commit id on the artifact and in the running process.

sections.label: Pipeline
sections.html:
Pipeline

The pipeline is the only path to production. If someone can still shell in and patch a server, the pipeline is a suggestion. Steps should be visible: build, test, publish, deploy, and a check that the new version is serving.

A green pipeline that never looks at the running system will ship a process that starts and then fails its first request.

sections.label: Environments
sections.html:
Environments

Development, a shared test environment, and production should differ by configuration, not by a mystery set of manual steps. Secrets stay out of the repository. Data in test is either synthetic or carefully reduced. Production data does not travel to a laptop.

Name who is allowed to deploy where. Production is a smaller group, and the action is still a recorded change, not a private click.

sections.label: After release
sections.html:
After release

Watch the new version, not only the cluster. Error rate, latency, and a business signal such as completed checkouts. Keep the previous version ready so rollback is a deploy, not a reconstruction.

Write down what you learned when a release hurts. The next pipeline check should catch that class of mistake. An incident that only lives in chat will happen again.

case-study.title: Case Study
case-study.deck: A case study is useful when it shows the constraint, not only the architecture diagram. These notes are a way to read one, and a place to file the next one.

sections.label: How to read one
sections.html:
How to read one

Start with the question the system had to answer, and the limit it could not ignore: latency, cost, a regulation, a team size, a traffic spike. The boxes on the diagram are the answer to that limit. Without the limit, the diagram is fashion.

Add a new case here as its own subsection when you have those facts. A title, the constraint, the design, and the outcome are enough. A slide full of product names is not.

sections.label: Constraint
sections.html:
Constraint

Write the constraint in one sentence. "Checkout must answer in under 200 milliseconds." "Two teams must deploy without waiting for each other." "The audit trail cannot be edited." If you cannot say it, you cannot judge the design.

Also write what was deliberately left out. A system that ignores search, or ignores multi-region, is not incomplete if that was the deal. It is incomplete if readers are not told.

sections.label: Design
sections.html:
Design

Name the few parts that carry the constraint. A cache in front of a catalog. A queue between payment and fulfillment. A single service that owns the ledger. Resist listing every sidecar.

  • What data is the source of truth.
  • What is allowed to be stale.
  • How a request is identified from the edge to the store.

sections.label: What broke
sections.html:
What broke

Every honest case has a failure. A cache that served a price after it changed. A queue that grew until orders were hours late. A rollout that passed health checks and still dropped payments. Record the symptom, the cause, and the change that followed.

A case with no failure mode is an advertisement. Treat it as incomplete.

sections.label: What to copy
sections.html:
What to copy

Copy the decision, not the vendor list. If your constraint matches, the shape may match. If your traffic, team, or data rules do not, leave the shape alone. Write one line: "Use this when…" and "Do not use this when…".

File the next study as a new section in this page. Link it from the left navigation, keep the same four questions, and push the page. The home card already points here.

learning-path.title: Learning Path
learning-path.deck: Read these notes in an order that builds a small system, not in the order the cards happen to sit on the home page.

sections.label: Suggested order
sections.html:
Suggested order

Do not try to finish every page before you build anything. One pass through the vocabulary, one small design, then the notes that explain how that design is shipped and how it fails.

  1. Cloud Fundamental, so the words for place, compute, storage, and identity are shared.
  2. Architect Design Patterns, so a local mess and a system-wide style are not confused.
  3. Microservices, only after you can say what must deploy apart.
  4. Kubernetes and DevOps, so the design can be run and changed.
  5. Case Study, to test the design against someone else's constraint.
  6. AI / ML, when a model is actually part of the decision, not as a first step.

sections.label: Vocabulary
sections.html:
Vocabulary

Spend the first pass on names you will reuse: region, request and limit, service boundary, pipeline, readiness. If a term is fuzzy, stay on that section until you can explain it without the page open.

Skip ahead only when the current section is not the problem you have. A team already running a cluster does not need to pretend they have never seen a pod. They do need the failure notes.

sections.label: Shape a system
sections.html:
Shape a system

Pick one workflow you know, such as placing an order or publishing a document. Write the constraint, the data owner, and the one dependency that would hurt if it were slow. Then open the pattern and microservice notes and see which split you actually need.

A learning design that needs five services on day one is practicing diagrams. Two processes and a database will teach more.

sections.label: Run and change it
sections.html:
Run and change it

Put the small system somewhere you can deploy twice. Use the DevOps notes for the pipeline and the Kubernetes notes if the runtime is a cluster. Change one thing, watch one signal, and roll it back on purpose.

The point is the loop, not the platform logo. A single virtual machine with a repeatable deploy still counts.

sections.label: Go deeper
sections.html:
Go deeper

After the loop works, return to the section that felt thin. Add a subsection on that topic page rather than starting a second notebook. A case study belongs on the Case Study page, in the same four questions: constraint, design, what broke, what to copy.

When a new shelf is large enough for its own card, add the folder, link it from the home page, and push to main. The deploy workflow publishes the new tile.

system-design.title: System Design
system-design.deck: Beginner-friendly case studies that explain how familiar systems work, what they optimize, and where their designs fail.

sections.label: Twitter / X
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Twitter / X is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Timeline fan-out — push posts to follower timelines for fast reads
  • Pull vs push — choose based on follower count and activity
  • Caching — keep hot timelines close to readers
  • Search — index text and hashtags separately

How a request moves

A user publishes a post through an API. The service stores the post and emits an event. Workers copy a lightweight post reference into follower timeline caches for ordinary accounts. When a celebrity has millions of followers, the system usually avoids copying to everyone and merges that account—s recent posts at read time.

A beginner-friendly design

Use a post store, a follow graph, a timeline cache, and a search index. A read service merges cached entries with a small set of high-follower accounts, removes deleted or blocked posts, and returns a cursor rather than a page number.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A celebrity post can create a fan-out storm. Cache stampedes, deleted content, and uneven partitions are common hazards. The design needs queue backpressure, cache expiry, and a way to rebuild a timeline from the source of truth.

Key takeaway: Timeline reads are optimized by moving work to publish time, but very large fan-out is better handled lazily.

sections.label: YouTube
sections.html:
What this system teaches

YouTube is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Upload pipeline — accept large files reliably
  • Transcoding — create multiple resolutions and codecs
  • CDN — serve video from a nearby edge
  • Adaptive bitrate — change quality as bandwidth changes

How a request moves

The client uploads directly to object storage using a resumable session. A metadata service records the upload and sends a job to a media queue. Workers validate, scan, transcode, package segments, and publish a manifest. Viewers fetch the manifest and segments through a CDN.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep original media immutable in object storage. Store metadata in a database, job state in a durable queue, and derived files under versioned keys. A player starts at a safe bitrate and switches representations using measured buffer and network speed.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Transcoding is expensive and can fail halfway through. Upload retries must not duplicate files, manifests should not point to incomplete outputs, and CDN invalidation must be controlled when a video changes.

Key takeaway: Video delivery is mostly a storage, asynchronous processing, and edge caching problem—not a single giant application server.

sections.label: Netflix
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Netflix is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Microservices — isolate business capabilities
  • Open Connect CDN — place content near viewers
  • Resilience — tolerate partial failures
  • Playback control — protect the viewing path

How a request moves

A client requests a title and playback session. Control-plane services authorize the user, choose a title rendition, and return nearby CDN locations. The client downloads small segments from the edge while telemetry flows back separately.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep playback reads short and cacheable. Use independent services for catalog, identity, recommendations, and playback authorization, but avoid making every video segment depend on them. Pre-position popular content and use timeouts, retries with limits, and fallbacks for nonessential features.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A dependency outage should not stop an already authorized stream. Bad retries can overload a failing service, and stale catalog data is safer than an unavailable browse page during a partial outage.

Key takeaway: Resilience comes from removing unnecessary dependencies from the critical path and placing bytes close to users.

sections.label: Uber
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Uber is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Geospatial indexing — find nearby drivers
  • Dispatch — match riders and drivers
  • ETA — estimate travel time
  • Location updates — process moving entities

How a request moves

A rider sends pickup and destination coordinates. The dispatch service searches nearby driver cells, filters unavailable drivers, estimates routes and arrival times, and proposes a trip. Driver location updates continuously refresh the spatial index while the trip state is stored durably.

A beginner-friendly design

Partition the map into cells such as H3-like hexagons. Keep recent driver positions in a fast geo store, but keep trip and payment state in a transactional database. Use a state machine so a driver cannot be assigned to two trips.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

GPS updates are noisy, drivers cross partitions, and two dispatchers may race. Leases, idempotent assignment commands, fencing tokens, and a fallback to a wider search radius prevent duplicate or missing assignments.

Key takeaway: Separate fast-changing location data from durable trip state, then make assignment a serialized decision.

sections.label: WhatsApp
sections.html:
What this system teaches

WhatsApp is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Chat delivery — route messages to recipients
  • Presence — show approximate online state
  • Receipts — track delivered and read states
  • Erlang-style concurrency — handle many connections

How a request moves

A sender connects to a gateway, which authenticates the session and accepts a message. The message is durably queued for each recipient device. Delivery and read acknowledgements update message state, while presence is published as short-lived information.

A beginner-friendly design

Use connection gateways for long-lived sessions, a message store keyed by conversation and sequence, and queues for offline recipients. Presence should have a TTL and should not be treated as durable truth. Encrypt message content so routing services need only metadata.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A phone can disconnect after the server accepts a message. Duplicate delivery, reconnect storms, out-of-order acknowledgements, and a slow offline recipient all require explicit state and retry rules.

Key takeaway: Reliable chat is a durable queue plus a connection service; —online— is a hint, not a guarantee.

sections.label: LinkedIn
sections.html:
What this system teaches

LinkedIn is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Feed ranking — select and order relevant posts
  • Connection graph — model relationships
  • Kafka — move activity as events
  • Fan-out — build candidate feeds

How a request moves

A member publishes an activity. An event stream distributes it to candidate-generation, ranking, notification, and analytics consumers. A feed request reads recent candidates, applies permissions and ranking features, and returns a cursor.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep the social graph separate from feed materialization. Events should be replayable so a new ranking model can rebuild candidates. Cache feature data, but record the model version used for ranking to make behavior explainable.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Events can arrive late or twice, privacy changes can invalidate old candidates, and ranking work can become expensive. Consumers need offsets, deduplication, versioned features, and a delete propagation path.

Key takeaway: An activity feed is an event-driven read model: the graph supplies candidates and ranking decides what deserves attention.

sections.label: Instagram
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Instagram is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Photo feed — combine media and relationships
  • Sharding — spread users and posts
  • ID generation — create sortable unique IDs
  • Object storage — keep large media outside the database

How a request moves

The client uploads a photo to object storage and sends metadata to an API. A media worker creates thumbnails. Feed workers or a read-time query select posts from followed accounts, while a CDN serves the image bytes.

A beginner-friendly design

Use a user-sharded metadata store, globally unique IDs, and object storage for originals and derivatives. Keep feed rows small: author, post ID, timestamp, and media key. Generate thumbnails once and cache them at the edge.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Hot users create uneven feed work, image processing may finish after the post is created, and deleted or private media can remain in caches. Version media keys and check authorization before issuing URLs.

Key takeaway: Separate metadata from blobs, and make the feed point to immutable media variants.

sections.label: Facebook social graph
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Facebook social graph is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • TAO-style graph access — optimize relationship reads
  • Graph storage — represent objects and edges
  • Cache consistency — keep popular relationships available
  • Read-heavy design — favor fast traversal

How a request moves

A profile, page, or post is an object. Friendship, membership, and reactions are edges. A graph request reads object and edge data through a cache-aware graph layer, falling back to storage when needed.

A beginner-friendly design

Model common traversals explicitly, such as —friends of this person— or —members of this page,— instead of running arbitrary graph queries on the request path. Cache hot edges with invalidation events and keep a durable source of truth underneath.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Popular objects create hot keys, edge deletes can race with reads, and a cache can expose stale privacy state. Use bounded queries, cache versioning, and authorization checks at the edge of the graph API.

Key takeaway: A social graph is not just a database table; its access patterns should be designed as named traversals.

sections.label: Dropbox / Google Drive
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Dropbox / Google Drive is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • File chunking — upload pieces independently
  • Sync — reconcile local and remote changes
  • Deduplication — avoid storing identical content
  • Metadata — track names, folders, and versions

How a request moves

A client splits a file into chunks, hashes them, uploads missing chunks, and commits a manifest. Other devices receive a change notification and download missing chunks. The metadata service decides which version is current and reports conflicts.

A beginner-friendly design

Store chunks immutably in object storage and keep file trees, manifests, and permissions in a transactional metadata store. Use content hashes for deduplication, resumable uploads, and a per-file version sequence.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Two devices can edit the same file, a client can disappear during commit, and deleting metadata before garbage collection can lose shared chunks. Keep tombstones, conflict copies, leases, and delayed garbage collection.

Key takeaway: Synchronize metadata and immutable chunks separately; the manifest is the bridge between them.

sections.label: URL shortener
sections.html:
What this system teaches

URL shortener is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Hashing — map long URLs to short keys
  • Key generation — avoid collisions
  • Key-value stores — serve redirects quickly
  • Analytics — record clicks asynchronously

How a request moves

A create request validates a destination and allocates a short key. The key and destination are stored. A redirect lookup reads the key from a cache or key-value store and returns an HTTP redirect; click events are sent to an analytics queue.

A beginner-friendly design

Use a unique random or sequence-based key, a primary key-value record, and a cache with expiry. Keep analytics out of the redirect path. If custom aliases are supported, reserve them transactionally.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A hot link can overwhelm one cache entry, keys can collide, and malicious destinations can turn the service into a spam or phishing tool. Rate-limit creation, validate URLs, and make writes idempotent.

Key takeaway: The redirect path should do one tiny lookup; everything optional belongs off the critical path.

sections.label: Pastebin
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Pastebin is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Object storage — hold paste bodies
  • Expiry — remove content after a deadline
  • Read-heavy design — cache popular pastes
  • Abuse controls — protect a public service

How a request moves

A client submits text and receives an ID. Metadata records the owner, size, visibility, and expiry. Reads check the metadata and fetch the body from object storage or a cache. A sweeper removes expired metadata and schedules blob deletion.

A beginner-friendly design

Use immutable object keys and a metadata index. Put short pastes in a cache, enforce size limits before storage, and use lifecycle policies for expiry. Separate public, unlisted, and private access checks.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Expiry jobs can be delayed, a popular paste can become a hot key, and untrusted text may contain scripts or secrets. Escape output, enforce content security, and treat expiry as an authorization check as well as cleanup.

Key takeaway: Simple content sharing still needs lifecycle management, safe rendering, and a clear source of truth.

sections.label: Rate limiter
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Rate limiter is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Token bucket — allow bursts within a budget
  • Sliding window — measure recent request volume
  • Distributed counters — coordinate many gateways
  • Fairness — protect tenants from each other

How a request moves

A gateway identifies a caller and asks a limiter for a decision before forwarding the request. The limiter updates a counter or token balance with an atomic operation and returns allow or retry-later. Metrics record both accepted and rejected traffic.

A beginner-friendly design

Choose the algorithm from the product rule. Store small per-key state in a fast replicated store, use server-side time, and define what happens when the limiter store is unavailable. Add separate limits for IP, user, API key, and expensive operations.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Clock differences, hot keys, fail-open decisions, and retry storms can defeat a limiter. Use atomic scripts or compare-and-set, bounded TTLs, jittered retry-after values, and a documented emergency policy.

Key takeaway: A limiter is a policy with state; correctness depends on identity, time, atomicity, and failure behavior.

sections.label: Ticketmaster / BookMyShow
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Ticketmaster / BookMyShow is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Seat locking — reserve temporarily
  • Concurrency — prevent double booking
  • Flash-sale load — handle sudden demand
  • Queues — control admission

How a request moves

A user enters a waiting room, selects seats, and creates a short lease. The booking service atomically changes available seats to held, collects payment, and commits the order. An expiry worker releases abandoned holds.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep the seat inventory as the transactional authority. Use a database constraint or conditional update so only one hold succeeds. Put users behind an admission queue and make payment callbacks idempotent. Do not trust the browser to own a seat.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A payment can succeed while the browser times out, a hold can expire during payment, and a flash sale can overload every layer. Use idempotency keys, a durable order state machine, bounded hold windows, and queue backpressure.

Key takeaway: Scarce inventory requires serialized state transitions; queues protect the system before the database becomes the bottleneck.

sections.label: Airbnb
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Airbnb is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Search ranking — find relevant listings
  • Booking consistency — avoid overlapping reservations
  • Availability — model calendar state
  • Payments — commit money safely

How a request moves

Search reads denormalized listing and availability data. A booking request rechecks the dates transactionally, places a reservation hold, authorizes payment, and confirms the reservation. Search indexes update asynchronously after changes.

A beginner-friendly design

Store reservations with a constraint that prevents overlapping date ranges or use per-listing calendar locks. Separate search documents from booking truth. Use a saga for payment, notifications, and host updates.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Search can be stale just as availability changes, two guests can race for the same dates, and payment can fail after a hold. Make booking the final authority and expire holds safely.

Key takeaway: Fast search may be eventually consistent, but the booking decision must be strongly protected.

sections.label: Amazon e-commerce
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Amazon e-commerce is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Cart — maintain intent across sessions
  • Inventory — reserve stock
  • Order pipeline — move through states
  • Sagas — coordinate services without one giant transaction

How a request moves

A shopper adds items to a cart, checks out, and receives an order ID. The order service reserves inventory, requests payment, creates fulfillment work, and emits notifications. Each step records its state and compensates when a later step fails.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep cart storage flexible and order records immutable after confirmation. Inventory uses conditional reservations, not a cached count. Coordinate payment, stock, and shipment with an order state machine and outbox events.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Inventory may be oversold if reservations are not atomic, payment callbacks may repeat, and shipping can fail after payment. Use idempotent commands, compensating actions, and reconciliation jobs.

Key takeaway: An order is a long-running workflow; make every transition visible and retryable.

sections.label: Web crawler
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Web crawler is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • URL frontier — schedule what to crawl
  • Politeness — respect hosts and robots rules
  • Deduplication — avoid repeated pages
  • Distributed workers — scale fetches

How a request moves

Seed URLs enter a frontier. Scheduler workers choose eligible URLs by host, fetchers download them with timeouts, parsers extract links, and a deduplication store decides which URLs are new. Results go to storage or an indexing pipeline.

A beginner-friendly design

Partition scheduling by host so one site has a concurrency limit. Canonicalize URLs before hashing, keep retry metadata, and store fetch status separately from content. Use a durable queue so workers can restart.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Hosts can be slow or hostile, pages can create infinite URL spaces, and retries can become a denial of service. Enforce budgets, robots policy, maximum sizes, timeouts, and dead-letter queues.

Key takeaway: A crawler is a scheduler with rules, not just a loop that downloads links.

sections.label: Search autocomplete
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Search autocomplete is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Tries — match prefixes efficiently
  • Top-K — return the best completions
  • Caching — serve common prefixes quickly
  • Offline indexing — update suggestions safely

How a request moves

A user sends a short prefix on each keystroke. The service checks a cache, looks up the prefix in a compact trie or finite-state index, and returns a small ranked list. Offline jobs rebuild the index from query and catalog data.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep the hot index in memory at each replica and publish immutable versions. Rank by frequency, freshness, locale, and safety. Debounce client requests and cap prefix length and result count.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A popular prefix can overload replicas, a bad suggestion can be offensive, and an index rebuild can consume memory. Use cache limits, moderation filters, atomic version swaps, and fallbacks to a smaller index.

Key takeaway: Autocomplete is a read-optimized index that trades instant freshness for predictable latency.

sections.label: Spotify
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Spotify is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Audio streaming — deliver sequential segments
  • Recommendations — combine signals and models
  • Playlists — manage ordered user content
  • CDN caching — keep popular tracks near users

How a request moves

A client requests metadata and a playback token, then streams encrypted audio segments from a nearby edge. Playback events are written asynchronously and feed recommendation pipelines. Playlist edits update metadata and invalidate relevant caches.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep audio files immutable and encoded at multiple bitrates. Use a CDN for segments, a metadata store for playlists, and an event stream for listening history. Separate playback authorization from recommendation availability.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A CDN miss or origin outage should not stop every listener, and duplicate events can distort recommendations. Prewarm popular content, use short-lived playback tokens, and deduplicate event IDs.

Key takeaway: The user experience depends on a small control-plane decision followed by a highly cacheable data-plane stream.

sections.label: Slack / Discord
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Slack / Discord is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • WebSocket gateways — maintain live connections
  • Channels — route messages to members
  • Message storage — preserve history
  • Fan-out — notify many connected clients

How a request moves

A client opens a gateway connection and subscribes to channels. A message command is persisted first, then published to channel subscribers and offline notification workers. Reconnecting clients provide a cursor to catch up.

A beginner-friendly design

Use stateless gateways backed by a membership service and pub/sub bus. Store messages by channel and sequence number. Keep presence and typing indicators ephemeral; keep message history durable.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A channel may have millions of members, gateways may disconnect, and events may arrive twice. Use bounded fan-out, per-channel sequence numbers, replay cursors, and backpressure for slow clients.

Key takeaway: Real-time delivery is an optimization over durable history; clients must be able to reconnect and catch up.

sections.label: Zoom / Google Meet
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Zoom / Google Meet is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • WebRTC — real-time media transport
  • SFU vs MCU — choose media routing strategy
  • Signaling — negotiate participants and sessions
  • Bandwidth adaptation — keep calls usable

How a request moves

A client joins a meeting through signaling, exchanges session descriptions, and sends media to a selected media server. An SFU forwards streams without mixing them; clients choose which streams to decode. Signaling handles joins, leaves, mute state, and reconnects.

A beginner-friendly design

Use regional signaling and media placement, short-lived meeting credentials, and an SFU for large interactive rooms. Record media separately from the live path. Monitor packet loss, jitter, round-trip time, and active speakers.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

NAT traversal can fail, a media server can overload, and a participant may have poor bandwidth. Use TURN fallback, admission limits, adaptive layers, regional failover, and graceful video reduction.

Key takeaway: Video meetings are latency-sensitive distributed systems where quality is managed continuously rather than guaranteed once.

sections.label: Google Maps
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Google Maps is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Tile serving — render map regions efficiently
  • Routing graphs — calculate paths
  • Traffic data — update travel estimates
  • Geospatial indexing — locate nearby data

How a request moves

The client requests map tiles for a viewport and route information for a pair of coordinates. A tile service reads immutable, cached tiles. A routing service searches a road graph and combines it with traffic signals and historical speeds.

A beginner-friendly design

Partition tiles by zoom and coordinate, cache them at the edge, and version each map release. Keep routing graphs in memory at regional replicas. Process traffic as a stream and publish updated weights without rebuilding every client request.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Map data changes while users are navigating, routes can be expensive, and a hot city can overload one shard. Use bounded alternatives, graph partitioning, cache keys with versions, and fallbacks to historical traffic.

Key takeaway: Separate static geographic content from dynamic traffic and routing computation.

sections.label: Food delivery (Swiggy)
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Food delivery (Swiggy) is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Order lifecycle — track state across parties
  • Rider assignment — match supply and demand
  • ETA — combine kitchen and travel time
  • Location updates — follow active deliveries

How a request moves

A customer creates an order, the restaurant accepts it, and a dispatch service assigns a rider. Kitchen events update preparation time; rider GPS updates refresh the ETA. Payment, notifications, and support consume order events.

A beginner-friendly design

Use an order state machine with explicit transitions and an event log. Keep restaurant, rider, and customer services separate but avoid synchronous calls for every update. Use geospatial candidate search and a short lease for rider assignment.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Restaurants may reject orders, riders can go offline, and payment can be delayed. Reassign with bounded timers, make status events idempotent, and show uncertainty rather than inventing a precise ETA.

Key takeaway: The hard part is coordinating real-world actors whose state changes outside your process.

sections.label: Payment system (Stripe)
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Payment system (Stripe) is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Idempotency — safely retry payment requests
  • Ledgers — record money movement
  • Reconciliation — compare independent records
  • Webhooks — notify merchants asynchronously

How a request moves

A merchant submits a payment with an idempotency key. The payment service validates it, calls a processor, records an immutable attempt and ledger entries, and returns a stable result. Webhooks notify the merchant and reconciliation jobs compare processor reports.

A beginner-friendly design

Treat the ledger as append-only and derive balances from entries. Store the idempotency key with the final response. Model authorization, capture, refund, and dispute as separate states. Never use a mutable balance as the only audit trail.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Networks time out after the processor accepts a charge, webhooks arrive twice or out of order, and settlement totals can differ. Use idempotent handlers, signed events, retry queues, and human-visible reconciliation reports.

Key takeaway: Money systems need an auditable history and safe retries more than clever request throughput.

sections.label: Notification service
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Notification service is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Push/email/SMS fan-out — deliver through many providers
  • Retries — recover temporary failures
  • Priority queues — protect urgent messages
  • Preferences — respect user choice

How a request moves

An application emits a notification intent. A router checks preferences and templates, places channel-specific jobs on queues, and provider workers deliver them. Delivery receipts and failures update an attempt record.

A beginner-friendly design

Separate intent from delivery attempts. Use per-provider queues, exponential backoff with a cap, deduplication keys, and a dead-letter queue. Keep urgent security messages separate from bulk campaigns.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Providers throttle or fail, templates can be invalid, and retries can spam users. Enforce user-level frequency limits, classify permanent failures, and make opt-out checks happen close to delivery.

Key takeaway: Notification reliability means controlled retries and user respect, not sending the same message forever.

sections.label: Distributed message queue (Kafka)
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Distributed message queue (Kafka) is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Partitions — spread ordered logs
  • Replication — survive broker loss
  • Consumer groups — divide work
  • Offsets — resume processing

How a request moves

Producers append records to a partition chosen by key. Brokers replicate the log. Consumers in a group read assigned partitions, process records, and commit offsets. New consumers rebalance partition ownership.

A beginner-friendly design

Choose a key when per-entity order matters, set retention for replay needs, and monitor consumer lag. Make processing idempotent because a crash can occur after work but before offset commit. Replication is not a substitute for backups and recovery tests.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Hot keys overload one partition, rebalances pause work, and slow consumers grow lag. Use key distribution, bounded batches, cooperative rebalancing, and alerts tied to processing time.

Key takeaway: A log gives consumers a replayable sequence; application correctness still depends on offset and side-effect handling.

sections.label: Reddit
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Reddit is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Voting — aggregate many small writes
  • Ranking — order posts and comments
  • Nested comments — represent trees
  • Caching — serve popular communities

How a request moves

A user votes or comments. The write is recorded and an event updates score and ranking projections. A feed request reads candidate posts, applies community and moderation rules, and returns comments using bounded tree queries.

A beginner-friendly design

Keep raw votes and derived scores separate. Store comment parent IDs and materialize paths or depth-limited views. Cache hot community pages while rechecking moderation and deletion state.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Vote bursts can create hot rows, deep comment trees can become expensive, and ranking abuse can dominate good content. Use sharded counters, asynchronous score updates, depth limits, and anti-abuse signals.

Key takeaway: Feeds are projections over many independent actions; raw events make rebuilding and correcting rankings possible.

sections.label: Pinterest
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Pinterest is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Home feed — retrieve and rank pins
  • Recommendations — use content and behavior
  • Graph — connect users, boards, and pins
  • Sharding — spread very large collections

How a request moves

A user follows or saves a pin. Events update graph edges and recommendation features. The home feed service gathers candidates from follows, related pins, and trends, ranks them, and returns a cursor.

A beginner-friendly design

Store pin media in object storage, graph relationships in access-oriented stores, and feed results as a cacheable read model. Use offline jobs for expensive recommendations and online rules for freshness and safety.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

A popular pin creates hot edges, new users lack history, and content can be deleted after being cached. Use cold-start defaults, bounded candidate sets, cache invalidation, and policy checks before display.

Key takeaway: Recommendation systems need several candidate sources so an empty history does not become an empty product.

sections.label: Tinder
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Tinder is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Geo-matching — find nearby candidates
