  • Swipe consistency — record decisions once
  • Recommendations — rank a changing pool
  • Privacy — limit location exposure

How a request moves

A user requests a batch of candidates. The service filters by distance, preferences, prior swipes, and safety rules. A swipe is stored idempotently; a mutual like creates a match event and opens a conversation path.

A beginner-friendly design

Use coarse geospatial cells rather than exposing exact coordinates. Keep swipe decisions append-only with a uniqueness rule. Generate candidate batches asynchronously, then filter again at read time for freshness.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

The same candidate can be shown twice, a user can swipe while the pool changes, and exact locations can leak. Use stable IDs, deduplication, expiry, privacy-preserving distance checks, and moderation.

Key takeaway: Matching is a recommendation problem wrapped around a small but important set of durable decisions.

sections.label: Google Docs
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Google Docs is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Real-time collaboration — merge concurrent edits
  • OT vs CRDT — preserve user intent
  • Presence — show active collaborators
  • Version history — make changes recoverable

How a request moves

A client sends an operation against a document version. The collaboration server orders or transforms operations, broadcasts accepted changes, and stores checkpoints and an operation log. Clients apply remote edits and acknowledge their local ones.

A beginner-friendly design

Use a document session for low-latency coordination and a durable operation log for recovery. Operational Transformation can transform edits against a shared sequence; CRDTs encode convergence into the data model. Presence should be ephemeral and separate from document truth.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Clients disconnect, operations arrive late, and large documents make every edit expensive. Use reconnect cursors, snapshots, compaction, operation IDs, and a clear conflict policy for unsupported objects.

Key takeaway: Collaboration is a consistency problem: define the merge rule before optimizing the websocket path.

sections.label: Yelp / nearby places
sections.html:
What this system teaches

Yelp / nearby places is a useful case study because it turns a familiar product into a set of engineering decisions. Start with the user action, identify the data that must survive, and then decide which work can happen later.

  • Geohash — bucket nearby coordinates
  • Quadtrees — recursively divide space
  • Read-heavy search — optimize discovery
  • Ranking — combine distance and relevance

How a request moves

A user sends a location and filters. The service chooses nearby spatial cells, retrieves candidate businesses, applies opening-hours and category filters, ranks results, and returns details from a cache or database.

A beginner-friendly design

Index businesses by geospatial cells and keep search documents denormalized for fast reads. Query the current cell plus neighboring cells, widening the radius when results are sparse. Update reviews and opening hours asynchronously but recheck critical availability fields.

Data, scale, and consistency

Keep the first version simple: separate the request path from background work, measure the slowest dependency, and store an identifier that makes retries safe. Add replicas and caches only after the access pattern is visible. Decide which values may be briefly stale and which action must be serialized, such as a payment or seat reservation.

What can go wrong

Cell boundaries can miss edge results, a city center can become a hot partition, and stale hours frustrate users. Query neighbors, split hot cells, cache carefully, and timestamp freshness.

Key takeaway: Nearby search is a bounded spatial lookup followed by ranking—not a full scan of every place.
